# Epigenetic Dysregulation and the Etiology of Spina Bifida

**Authors:** Tabitha Lumour-Mensah; Susan Korrick; Bernardo Lemos; Maitreyi Mazumdar

**Affiliations:** aDepartment of Environmental Health, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston, MA 02115, United States of America | bChanning Division of Network Medicine, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA 02115, United States of America | cR. Ken Coit College of Pharmacy, The University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ 85721, United States of America | dDepartment of Neurology, Boston Children’s Hospital, Boston, MA 02115, United States of America

## Abstract

Spina bifida is a complex and multifactorial congenital defect driven by both genetic and environmental factors. As such, epigenetic studies of spina bifida present an opportunity to study the joint contribution of both genes and the environment in the development of this disorder. This review focuses specifically on epigenetic research that may help us to understand the ways in which dysregulation of the epigenome and downstream cellular processes can confer increased risk of spina bifida. To do so, we discuss the epigenetic regulation of genes linked to spina bifida risk among children born with the disorder and their parents. We also discuss pathways necessary for normal neural tube development and specific documented dysregulation of these pathways in individuals with spina bifida. We conclude that the epigenome plays an important role in spina bifida etiology and should be further studied in additional populations, and tissue types, as well as cellular and animal models.

## Background

### Epigenetics

Epigenetics is the study of modifiable modifications to the structure of the genome that drive gene expression without alteration of the genomic sequence itself. DNA methylation (Section 1.1.1), histone modifications (Section 1.1.2), and non-coding RNA interactions (Section 1.1.3) are the most well understood epigenetic mechanisms and represent key mechanisms by which the environment can modify biological function (Godfrey et al., 2016; Weinhold, 2006).

#### DNA methylation

DNA methylation refers to the addition of methyl groups to cytosine residues by DNA methyltransferase enzymes (DNMTs). The bulk of DNA methylation occurs at CpGs, a shorthand used to describe cytosine bases that are followed by guanine bases. Increased methylation at gene promoter regions is typically associated with decreased gene expression (Moore et al., 2012). However, methylation in gene bodies has been demonstrated to result in increased gene expression, indicating that the location of methylation plays an important role in the impact of DNA methylation on gene expression (Aran et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2014). DNA methylation also contributes to genomic stability through the silencing of transposable elements and other repetitive sequences that can insert into other parts of the genome or form secondary structures that interfere with DNA replication or cause DNA misalignments (Madireddy & Gerhardt, 2017; Moore et al., 2012; O’Dushlaine et al., 2005).

#### Histone modifications

Core histones are proteins around which the DNA molecule wraps itself. Histones can be modified in several ways that influence the packaging and accessibility of DNA in the cell nucleus. Histone modifications are diverse and include methylation, phosphorylation, ubiquitination and acetylation. Modifications to the tails of histones can affect how tightly they bind to DNA and in doing so affect the availability of the DNA to the transcriptional machinery (Moore et al., 2012). Histone modifications can occur at various sites on the histone protein and the effects of these histone modifications on gene expression is a function of the molecule attached to the histone, the number of molecules added to the histone tail and location of the modification (Fallah et al., 2021).

#### MicroRNA

Like DNA methylation and histone modifications, non-coding RNA molecules can affect gene expression across the genome. Non-coding RNA molecules are generally classified by size and their ability to function as RNA molecules without first being translated into proteins (Iyengar et al., 2014). MicroRNA (miRNA) are non-coding RNA that are typically between 21–23 nucleotides in length and can modify to both transcriptional and translational activity (O’Brien et al., 2018; Shang et al., 2023). Most commonly, miRNA molecules bind specific mRNAs and prevent their translation into proteins by inducing the degradation of mRNAs (Dave et al., 2023; Huntzinger & Izaurralde, 2011).

#### Epigenetics and disease

Given that these epigenetic modifications regulate gene expression, they are vital to key processes such as cell differentiation in stem cells and normal cellular function in fully differentiated cells (Di Tizio et al., 2018; Godfrey et al., 2016; Mohtat & Susztak, 2010). Notably, these epigenetic modifications are modifiable and allow cells to adapt to the environment. Relatedly, the epigenome is responsive to environmental features such as toxin exposure, diet, stress, physical activity (Bischoff-Ferrari et al., 2025; Bozack et al., 2020; Moosavi & Ardekani, 2016; X. Ren et al., 2010; Xu et al., 2023). Given the ability of the epigenome to respond to environmental stimuli and in turn affect biological function, study of epigenetic modifications and the epigenetic regulatory genes upstream of those epigenetic modifications can play an important role in our understanding of multifactorial disorders with both environmental and genetic causes.

### Spina bifida

Spina bifida is the most common neural tube defect (NTD), arising from the incomplete closure of the neural tube — a structure that later develops into the brain and spinal cord— during early embryogenesis (Copp et al., 2015). “Spina bifida” can be used to refer to either spina bifida occulta, meningocele, or myelomeningocele. Spina bifida occulta is the mildest form of the disorder in which there is a gap in the vertebrae that is covered by the skin. This form of spina bifida requires specialized imaging techniques (eg MRI) for diagnosis. Therefore, spina bifida occulta often goes undiagnosed because of its lack of visible malformation or clear symptoms. Furthermore, some evidence suggests that spina bifida occulta may resolve itself as the vertebral arch closes later in life (Urrutia et al., 2017).

Unlike spina bifida occulta, meningocele and myelomeningocele are clearly visible and more severe than spina bifida occulta. Meningocele is a form of spina bifida in which the gap in the vertebrae is accompanied by a visible protrusion containing cerebrospinal fluid. Myelomeningocele is the most severe manifestation of spina bifida and describes a form of the condition in which the nerves of the spinal cord and spinal fluid are contained in the protrusion that has formed as a result of the neural tube’s failure to close during gestation (Copp et al., 2015). These protruding nerves and fluid are covered by the meninges, the outermost protective layer of which is called the dura mater. The dura mater around the spinal cord is a single continuous layer composed of fibroblasts and a network of collagen and elastin fibers (Bican et al., 2013; Dorrier et al., 2021). Immune cells are embedded into this structural network of fibroblasts and fibers while the interior side of the dura mater is covered with flattened mesothelial cells (Dorrier et al., 2021; Møllgård et al., 2023). (Figure 1)

Prevalence of spina bifida varies significantly across regions with higher reported prevalences in the Eastern Mediterranean region, Southern Asia and Northern China (Zaganjor et al., 2016). While there is no singular known cause for the differences in prevalence across the globe, maternal folate deficiency is one of the most well-known risk factors for spina bifida as well as a necessary component of cellular epigenetic regulation (Chang et al., 2011; Crider et al., 2012; Kancherla et al., 2017). Relatedly, in a meta-analysis of global studies between 1985 and 2010, Atta and colleagues (2016) found that the average prevalence of spina bifida is 34 out of every 100,000 live births in regions that mandate folic acid fortification, whereas its prevalence is 48 out of every 100,000 live births in regions that do not mandate folic acid fortification (Atta et al., 2016). Further, there is evidence that folic acid supplementation can lower risk of neural tube defects among populations exposed to arsenic – a heavy metalloid linked with increased NTD risk (Pi et al., 2023).

## Epigenetics and spina bifida

The causes of spina bifida are a complex combination of genetic and environmental factors with current hypotheses describing a multifactorial threshold model (a.k.a., the multiple insult hypothesis) in which several genes and environmental factors act in concert to cause the failure of appropriate neural tube closure during development (Mohd-Zin et al., 2017; M. Wang et al., 2019). Mutations in genes that regulated epigenetic processes such as the addition of methyl groups to DNA have been implicated in a host of disorders including spina bifida (Klein et al., 2011; Mazumdar et al., 2015; Wilde et al., 2014). In addition to these epigenetic regulator genes, more than 300 genes play more direct roles in neural plate formation and neural tube closure (Nikolopoulou et al., 2017). In this paper, we seek to highlight a few key pathways and related genes in order to provide an overview of the role of the epigenome in neural tube closure and spina bifida. (Table 1 ; Figure 1)

### DNA methylation and spina bifida

Several genes have been associated with spina bifida risk, many of which have as their primary function the ability to regulate the expression of other genes in the genome (Sadhukhan et al., 2022; R. Wang et al., 2021; C. F. Wei et al., 2024). One such gene is DNMT1, the gene encoding DNA methyltransferase 1, the most prevalent DNMT enzyme across tissues, and the enzyme responsible for the maintenance of DNA methylation marks after successive mitotic cell divisions (Y. Ren, 2022). In addition to its function as a maintenance enzyme, DNMT1 has also been demonstrated to participate in de novo DNA methylation of oocytes (Y. Li et al., 2018). DNMT1 is also critical in the maintenance of methylation signatures and silencing of long terminal repeat retrotransposons during embryogenesis (Gaudet et al., 2004; Haggerty et al., 2021).

Importantly, maternal variants in DNMT1 in highly arsenic exposed human populations as well as reduced expression of DNMT1 in both mothers to children born with spina bifida and in the children themselves have been associated with increased spina bifida risk when compared to controls (Sadhukhan et al., 2022; C. F. Wei et al., 2024). Like DNMT1, polymorphisms in DNMT3a, a gene encoding another DNA methyltransferase enzyme, are associated with increased risk of spina bifida among children who also had higher drinking water arsenic exposure (Mazumdar et al., 2015). The case for a link between DNA methyltransferase function and incomplete neural tube closure leading to spina bifida is further evidenced by reduced expression of DNMT1 and DNMT3a an experimental model of the disorder in chick embryos with homocysteine induced NTDs (R. Wang et al., 2021).

### Histone modifications and spina bifida

In addition to genes encoding DNMTs, there is evidence of aberrant histone modification among spina bifida cases. Increased acetylation of histone H4 has been observed in human fetal brain tissues taken from embryos with failed neural tube closure when compared to healthy control samples (D. Li et al., 2019). The exact mechanisms by which these increases in histone acetylation increase neural tube defect risk are yet to be fully explained. However, H4 acetylation impacts genes expression by weakening the association between histones and DNA. Consequently, the increased H4 acetylation associated with spina bifida likely indicates an increase in transcription of affected neural tube closure genes (Fallah et al., 2021).

### microRNA and spina bifida

In addition, several miRNAs have been implicated in spina bifida development. In experimentally induced spina bifida in animals and in observational epidemiological studies, miR-124 and miR-9 have been found to be under expressed in spina bifida cases when compared to counterparts without spina bifida (Buczyńska et al., 2024; Qin et al., 2016, 2017; R. Wang et al., 2021; J. J. Zhao et al., 2008). Specifically, the miR-124 family of genes and miR-9/9* are regulatory micro RNAs that are highly expressed in the central nervous system (Kozuka et al., 2019; Miska et al., 2004; Sempere et al., 2004).

Notably, miR-124 is an important regulator of SOX9, a transcription factor associated with neural crest formation during the embryonic period (Cheung & Briscoe, 2003; Vogel & Wegner, 2020; Vong et al., 2015). In addition, knock out experiments to evaluate the role of miR-124 in spina bifida have indicated that the absence of miR-124 is sufficient to cause spina bifida in chick embryos (R. Wang et al., 2021).

## Dysregulated biological pathways associated with spina bifida

### Spina bifida and folate metabolism

Low maternal folate has been well established as an important risk factor for spina bifida (Ahrens et al., 2011; Atta et al., 2016). Relatedly, genes involved in folate metabolism may play a role in several stages of neural tube closure due to the role of these genes in the availability of the methyl groups necessary for both DNA and histone modification. Indeed, maternal polymorphisms in SLC19A1 and MTHFD1 are associated with increased risk of spina bifida, a trend also replicated among individuals with higher arsenic exposure (Mazumdar et al., 2015; Pangilinan et al., 2012).

In addition to these observations of alterations in folate metabolism genes among mothers to children with spina bifida, low folate has been demonstrated to disrupt GNAS methylation in both spermatozoa and oocytes (L. Wang et al., 2017). Gnas expression is complex and can be paternally imprinted (monoallelic) or expressed by both maternal and paternal copies (biallelic) depending on the tissue and the subunit of GNAS being expressed (Peters & Williamson, 2008). Further, aberrant GNAS methylation in sperm, oocytes and placenta have been associated with failed neural tube closure resulting in spina bifida (L. Wang et al., 2017; X. Zhang et al., 2015).

### Regulation of genes associated with sonic hedgehog signaling pathway

Normal function of the sonic hedgehog signaling (shh) pathway is necessary for several stages of embryogenesis, including neural tube closure (Brooks et al., 2020; Ingham & McMahon, 2001). While its direct role in spina bifida etiology has yet to be completely understood, the SOX18 gene is a target of the sonic hedgehog signaling pathway and direct evidence of the link between the gene and spina bifida has been observed through the disruption of neural tube formation in zebrafish embryos injected with Sox18 mRNA (Petrovic et al., 2015; Rochtus et al., 2016).

In addition to the influence of the sonic hedgehog signaling on SOX18 expression, GLI2, a direct downstream effector of the pathway is expressed throughout the neural tube (C. B. Bai et al., 2002; Hui et al., 1994). In addition, there is evidence that GLI2 dysregulation can induce incomplete neural tube closure in animal models (Pan et al., 2008). Specifically, spina bifida is associated with GLI2 hypermethylation and consequent low expression of GLI2 in brain tissue (X. L. Lu et al., 2016).

In contrast, GLI2 is upregulated in vitro by a form of H3K79 modification called homocysteinylation in which homocysteine is added to histone proteins, indicating that dysfunction of multiple epigenetic pathways may act in concert to dysregulated GLI2 to cause incomplete neural tube closure (Gu et al., 2021). It is also notable that elevated homocysteine levels are associated with folate deficiency independently of GLI2 expression (Kaye et al., 2020; Wald et al., 2001). Due to this relationship with folate metabolism, this finding may indicate another potential pathway through which folate deficiency and incomplete neural tube closure are linked.

### Regulation of genes associated with planar cellular polarity pathway

The planar cellular polarity (PCP) pathway is involved in several components of embryonic development. Notably, PCP signaling plays a key role in the process of convergent extension and neural tube formation after gastrulation (Shi, 2022; Sun et al., 2016; M. Wang et al., 2019; Zeng & Liu, 2023). Relatedly, SNPs in PCP signaling pathway genes have been demonstrated to be more common in people with spina bifida compared to age and sex matched controls (Liu et al., 2022). As a component of the PCP pathway, FZD3 is a gene in the PCP pathway that is involved in the coordination of cell migration through the establishment of planar cell polarity in the neural plate. Even in the absence of SNPs in the FZD3 gene, DNA methylation has been demonstrated to be higher in fetuses with spina bifida compared to those without. In addition, decreased transcription of FZD3 has been observed in in vitro experiments of human cells exposed to 5-azadCyD – a known disruptor of neural tube closure (Shangguan et al., 2015).

DVL2 is another protein with a role in the PCP pathway further downstream of the FZD family of proteins (Ortiz-Cruz et al., 2021; Z. Zhang et al., 2024). DVL1 has been found to be significantly decreased in fetuses with spina bifida in a Chinese cohort (S. Chen et al., 2017). The association between DLV2 and neural tube closure was further validated by the observation that mouse cells treated with methotrexate (MTX)—a compound demonstrated to induce NTDs also had decreased Dvl1 and Dvl2 expression (S. Chen et al., 2017; J. Zhao et al., 2013). Notably, MTX inhibits folate metabolism, a further indication of the role of folate related pathways on healthy neural tube closure (Muller et al., 2023). (Figure 2)

### Regulation of genes associated with WNT pathway

WNT pathway genes have been consistently implicated in spina bifida (J. Li et al., 2021; Ortiz-Cruz et al., 2021; Shi, 2022; M. Wang et al., 2019). As was demonstrated to be the case with the DVL1 and DVL2 genes in the PCP pathway, histone acetylation seems to be an important epigenetic mechanism associated with the aberrant expression of these genes observed in individuals with spina bifida. However, unlike FZD3, DVL1 and DVL2, WNT2b and WNT7b have been observed to be upregulated in tissues from individuals with spina bifida. Further, observation of H3K4 acetylation enrichment, reduction in trimethylated H3K27 and WNT2b and WNT7b hypomethylation in spina bifida support the case for epigenetic dysregulation of these genes contributing to increased spina bifida risk (B. Bai et al., 2015).

### Regulation of genes associated with neurotrophic signaling pathways

Neurotrophins are key growth factors that regulate neural growth and differentiation expressed during early embryonic development (Bernd, 2018). Specifically, the BDNF gene encodes a neurotrophin that regulates differentiation of embryonic neural precursors cells and embryonic stem cells (Bernd, 2018). This gene has been found to be hypermethylated in placental tissue samples belonging to individuals diagnosed with spina bifida and in mouse models with valproic acid induced neural tube defects (Finnell et al., 2003; X. Zhang et al., 2015). Importantly, BDNF plays a role in proliferation and differentiation during neural tube development in a chick animal model and has been demonstrated to participate in spinal cord repair in a mouse model (Jungbluth et al., 1997; X. Wei et al., 2022).

### Regulation of genes associated with apoptosis pathways

Programmed cell death through apoptosis is a part of neural tube closure and there is evidence of aberrant apoptotic activity in embryos with incomplete neural tube closure (Cecconi et al., 2008; X. Wei et al., 2012). Namely, an experimental study of mice with spina bifida induced by treatment with all-trans-retinoic acid (ATRA) has demonstrated epigenetic dysregulation of several genes associated with apoptosis with 13 such genes being upregulated while nucleolar protein 3—an apoptosis inhibitor was upregulated (Wan et al., 2018).

PEG10 is a paternally imprinted gene hypermethylated and lowly expressed in brain tissue taken from spina bifida patients. Despite its association with spina bifida in a population in northern China with a relatively high incidence of neural tube defects, its role in neural tube closure is not well defined (X. Lu et al., 2021). However, PEG10 does play an important role in placental function and aberrant apoptosis (Lux et al., 2010). Given this, PEG10 repression may impact spina bifida risk by disrupting apoptosis. While apoptotic cells can be found within the neural tube during its closure in early embryogenesis of mice, the exact role of apoptosis remains unclear (Massa et al., 2009). Increased apoptosis may lead to a decrease in cells necessary for the cell migration and specialization during neural tube closure while decreased apoptosis in neural precursor cells may disrupt the cellular homeostasis necessary for differentiation and consequent neural tube closure (Cecconi et al., 2008; Huang et al., 2021; Massa et al., 2009).

In addition to this role of PEG10 in apoptosis, PEG10 plays a key role in placental formation and the maintenance of placental vasculature throughout pregnancy (Abed et al., 2019; H. Chen et al., 2015; Shiura et al., 2023). Given the key role of the placenta in the environment of the developing fetus, disruption to PEG10 and consequent disruptions to nutrient transfer between mother and fetus which may, in turn, impact the availability of folate and other micronutrients necessary for successful neural tube closure (Shiura et al., 2021).

## Conclusions

Given the strength of evidence for the multiple insult hypothesis for spina bifida, it is important to emphasize that the genes discussed in this review should be viewed as components of a larger set of risk factors leading up to spina bifida. That said, it is also important to highlight the role of epigenetic regulation as a key mechanism whereby some genes confer risk of spina bifida and which may allow us to understand the nexus of genetics and environmental factors. Further work is needed to expand our understanding of which genes that are differentially expressed in those born with spina bifida across different populations with differing levels of exposures known to increase spina bifida risk. In tandem with further population-based research, experimental work is necessary to understand which of these epigenetic changes may be causative of neural tube defects. In doing so, we can work to better predict risk before spina bifida occurs, to design appropriate preventive interventions such as folic acid supplementation in folate deficient populations or to leverage upcoming epigenetic therapies.

# Evidence of reduced gestational age in response to in utero arsenic exposure and implications for aging trajectories of the newborn

**Authors:** Tabitha Lumour-Mensah; Bernardo Lemos

**Affiliations:** 1.Department of Environmental Health, Harvard School of Public Health, Boston, MA | 2.R. Ken Coit College of Pharmacy, Department of Pharmacology and Toxicology, The University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ | 3.Coit Center for Longevity and Neurotherapeutics, The University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ

## Abstract

Arsenic exposure is associated with a plethora of age-related health outcomes of disparate etiology. However, evidence of the impact of arsenic on aging remains limited. Here, we investigated the utility of these clocks in two different populations and the impact of maternal arsenic exposure during pregnancy on epigenetic gestational age at birth. To do this, we examined publicly available DNA methylation data and estimated gestational age across five gestational clocks in two unrelated human populations. These populations also differ in the extent of arsenic exposure and the targeted tissue of analysis (cord blood and placental tissue). Our results indicate that same-tissue clocks produce gestational age estimates that are more highly correlated with clinical gestational age. Interestingly, our results also indicate that arsenic exposure is associated with gestational age, with higher arsenic exposures associated with decreased gestational age. We also applied two pediatric clocks to evaluate infant biological age in the same samples. The data is suggestive of higher pediatric age in infants exposed to higher arsenic levels during gestation. Taken altogether, our findings are consistent with past work indicating that that in utero arsenic exposure is associated with decreased gestational maturity as characterized by infant outcomes such as low birthweight and lung underdevelopment and dysfunction in arsenic exposed infants. The findings are also consistent with arsenic exposure setting infants on a trajectory of accelerated epigenetic aging that starts at birth.

## Introduction

Arsenic is a carcinogen and contaminant found in drinking water, foods, and air. Once in the body, arsenic can pass through the placenta into the developing fetus (Jin et al., 2006; Markowski et al., 2011; Punshon et al., 2015). Inhalation exposure occurs via arsenic-containing particulate matter and dust in certain regions of the United States (e.g. Arizona and Utah) and across the globe. In drinking water, arsenic often occurs at levels that exceed the 10 ppb maximum contaminant level (MCL) that has been designated by the World Health Organization as an acceptable level for consumption. The issue is particularly concerning in private water wells in regions with high arsenic containing ground water. This is the case, for instance, in the US state of New Hampshire, as well as regions in Mexico and Bangladesh. Relatedly, there are well documented adverse impacts of arsenic on both maternal and fetal health outcomes, including gestational diabetes, preterm birth, decreased pulmonary function and infant mortality (Kile et al., 2016; Quansah et al., 2015; Ramsey et al., 2013; Salmeri et al., 2020). In addition, in utero arsenic exposure has been associated with genetic damage and epigenetic perturbation in newborns (Broberg et al., 2014; Cardenas et al., 2015; Kantisin et al., 2022; Lumour-Mensah & Lemos, 2023; Navasumrit et al., 2019; Pilsner et al., 2012). Relatedly, past work has indicated that DNA methylation in cord blood may mediate the relationship between in utero arsenic exposure and clinical gestational age (Bozack et al., 2018).

In addition, experimental evidence corroborates epidemiological evidence indicating that arsenic can impact gestational development through the epigenome. For example, mouse studies in which pregnant mice were exposed to inorganic arsenic found that pups exposed during gestation displayed several changes to their epigenome; one of the most significantly impacted functions was the canonical Wnt-signaling pathway that regulates fetal development and birthweight (Colwell et al., 2023; Tsang et al., 2012). In addition to these findings about birthweight, there have been experimental studies in mice that have indicated that newborn lung function, another important indicator of gestational development, is also linked to arsenic through modifications in the epigenome (Ramsey et al., 2013).

In determining risk for age-related health outcomes, chronological age can be a useful proxy for cellular aging and senescence that results in attrition of cellular and bodily functions. However, a major limitation in this use of chronological age as a proxy for biological function is substantial individual biological heterogeneity in aging (Duan et al., 2022; Ryan & Calen Ryan, 2021). For this reason, DNA based epigenetic clocks may be a better estimate of biological age and consequent risk for age-related outcomes including cancers than traditional chronological age (Horvath, 2013; Ryan & Calen Ryan, 2021; Wang and Lemos 2019). Thus, DNA methylation-based epigenetic clocks are a promising step in DNA methylation research to allow evaluation of biological age and enable the assessment of the impacts of environmental exposures on biological age.

The DNA methylation clocks most relevant to this study can be grouped into gestational clocks and pediatric clocks. However, it is important to highlight that these classes of clocks seek to measure distinct features. While pediatric clocks were specifically developed to measure biological age in children and young adults, gestational clocks were specifically developed to measure fetal development and maturity as indicated by gestational age (Bohlin et al., 2016; Knight et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2019; Mayne et al., 2017; McEwen et al., 2020; J. Wang & Zhou, 2021; Wu et al., 2019). As such, gestational clocks may present an opportunity to link certain in utero environmental exposures with fetal development to better understand the mechanisms by which these exposures impact health (Lee et al., 2019). Indeed, previous work has indicated that epigenetic clocks are both predictive of length of gestation and sensitive to perturbations in the gestational environment (Euclydes et al., 2022; Ladd-Acosta, Vang, Barrett, Bulka, Miller, et al., 2023; Song et al., 2022).

Here we use cord blood and placental tissue samples from neonates to assess whether in utero arsenic exposure might impact gestational maturity as estimated by gestational epigenetic clocks and pediatric aging as estimated by epigenetic clocks built for younger aged individuals. We hypothesize that in utero arsenic exposures might be associated with decreased gestational age and maturity as well epigenetic age acceleration in pediatric clocks at birth.

## Materials and Methods

### Sample Populations and Data Sources

We analyzed two publicly available datasets that included measurements of maternal urinary arsenic levels during pregnancy as well as DNA methylation data for the infants. It is important to note that because the urinary excretion is the body’s primary method of removing arsenic, urinary arsenic is a useful indicator for arsenic exposure (Douillet et al., 2023). However, urinary arsenic levels are most reflective of recent exposures over the span of the previous days or weeks (Calderon et al., 1999; García Salcedo et al., 2022). That said, urinary arsenic levels measured at one time point have been taken as a proxy for arsenic exposure throughout pregnancy in this work because the presumed primary source of arsenic in these populations is through contaminated drinking water. Since these are relatively stable, urinary arsenic is also presumed to present a relatively stable measurement of general arsenic exposure during pregnancy.

Further details about both populations included in this analysis can be found in respective papers published by the initial investigators (Green et al., 2016; Punshon et al., 2015; Rojas et al., 2015). However, key details of both populations relevant to our analyses are summarized here (Table 1).

#### United States Population

Data from US population included in our analyses are comprised of 343 infants from New Hampshire, USA collected as part of a New Hampshire Birth Cohort study. Gestational arsenic exposure in this subset was defined as maternal urinary arsenic levels as measured between the 24th and 28th weeks of pregnancy (Green et al., 2016; Punshon et al., 2015). DNA methylation in in fetal-side placental tissue was measured using the Illumina 450K array (Illumina, San Diego, CA).

#### Mexico Population

Data from a population in Mexico included in our analysis are comprised of 38 infants from Gómez Palacio, Mexico collected as part of the Biomarkers of Exposure to ARsenic (BEAR) Birth Cohort. Gestational arsenic exposure here is defined as maternal urinary arsenic levels as measured at delivery (Rojas et al., 2015). In addition, DNA methylation in infants was measured using the Illumina 450K array in cord blood (Illumina, San Diego, CA).

### Epigenetic Clocks

While there have been general epigenetic clocks developed with the goal of being used in a wide range of tissues and ages, they are often inappropriate for specific purposes. Here, we have elected to assess gestational age using clocks that are designed specifically for assessing (i) gestational age and maturity in placenta and cord blood and (ii) epigenetic pediatric age clocks designed specifically for young individuals (Bohlin et al., 2016; Knight et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2019; Mayne et al., 2017; McEwen et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2019). The focus on pediatric clocks is important because alternative post-natal epigenetic clocks of aging are not optimized for newborns and are therefore likely to be less predictive of pediatric age in cord blood and placenta tissues (McEwen et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2019). Further, we seek to evaluate whether there might be a role for clocks that are less predictive of clinical chronological age due to tissue type mismatch but remain sensitive to environmental perturbation.

Each of the clocks used here utilizes a set of CpGs that investigators have found to be predictive of gestational or chronological age across several datasets. CpGs present in each clock are dependent on the features of the individuals on whose epigenomes these clocks were trained and the quantitative methods by which each clock is constructed. More detailed discussion about the construction and logic underlying the clocks selected can be found elsewhere (Bohlin et al., 2016; Knight et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2019; Mayne et al., 2017; McEwen et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2019). However, some pertinent features of each clock are included here (Table 2).

#### Gestational clocks:

Given the unique features of the fetal epigenome, there have been multiple clocks developed specifically for gestational age. The clocks that we will be applying in our analyses were trained on DNA methylation data from cord blood or placenta samples. Of the gestational clocks that we applied here, two were developed using DNA methylation data from cord blood, namely the Bohlin clock (Bohlin et al., 2016) and the Knight clocks (Knight et al., 2016).

The Bohlin clock was trained in 1,753 infants from the Norwegian Mother and Child Birth Cohort Study. To construct this clock, DNA methylation was first measured using the Illumina 450K array. After this, linear regression was used to assess the relationship between CpG DNA methylation and clinical gestational age, controlling for cell type, child sex, maternal smoking, maternal age, and delivery type (cesarean section vs vaginal delivery). The CpGs with statistically significant associations with clinical gestational age were then included in a Lasso-type regression to identify the 96 CpGs that comprise this clock (Bohlin et al., 2016).

Unlike the Bohlin clock, the Knight clock was trained in DNA methylation data from both the Illumina 450K and 27K arrays. In addition, the Knight clock was built in infants with more diverse backgrounds. The trained data included populations that were majority Black as well as populations that were majority White. In addition, data was taken from individuals living in the US, Finland, Mexico, Spain, Australia and Denmark. To build this method of estimating gestational age, Knight and colleagues used elastic net regression-based methods. In addition, Knight and colleagues accounted for cell-type and study population to ultimately proposed a gestational age clock composed of 148 CpGs (Knight et al., 2016).

The three clocks proposed by Lee and colleagues (Lee et al., 2019) were all built using DNA methylation data taken from fetal-side placenta samples. These clocks were built using DNA methylation data generated with the Illumina 450K and EPIC arrays. The Control Placental Clock (hereafter referred to as Lee CPC) excluded complicated pregnancies such as those in which pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes and infant chromosomal abnormalities were present. This clock was trained in 963 placental samples and is composed of 546 CpGs. In contrast, the Robust Placental Clock (hereafter referred to as Lee RPC) was built using methylation data taken from 1,102 individuals including those with pregnancy complications that include diabetes and chromosomal abnormalities. The Lee RPC is composed of 558 CpGs. Lastly, the refined Robust Placental Clock (hereafter referred to as Lee ref RPC) was trained on a subset of the original Lee RPC (n=69) but was restricted to full term pregnancies. All 396 CpGs included in the Lee ref RPC were also included in the Lee RPC (Lee et al., 2019).

#### Pediatric clocks:

In addition, we decided to assess two clocks optimized for younger individuals. The first of these is the pediatric clock proposed by Wu and colleagues (hereafter referred to as the Wu clock) (Wu et al., 2019). In order to build this clock, Wu and colleagues evaluated the correlation between CpG methylation and chronological age (months) in 716 blood samples. These samples were derived from 11 methylation datasets of diverse racial and age composition. Across study populations, ages ranged from 9-212 months and DNA methylation was measured on the 27K and 450K Illumina arrays. The clock was built using penalized elastic net regression and resulted in clock composed of 111 CpGs (Wu et al., 2019).

The second pediatric clock evaluated here was the Pediatric-Buccal-Epigenetic (PedBE) clock proposed by McEwen and colleagues (McEwen et al., 2020). DNA methylation was assessed using the 450K and EPIC Illumina arrays. The clock was built using elastic net penalized regression on a training dataset of 1,032 individuals with an age range from 0 to 20 years. The final PedBE clock was composed of 94 CpGs (McEwen et al., 2020).

### Estimation of epigenetic gestational age and epigenetic pediatric age

Estimated age (gestational or pediatric) is based solely on DNA methylation at target CpGs, and is predicted independently of clinical gestational ages or chronological age. Furthermore, chronological age is defined as zero in the newborns studied here. In order to evaluate the ability of these clocks to predict clinical gestational age in different tissues and populations, we generated epigenetic age estimates for both the US and Mexico based populations in each of the five gestational clocks and both of the pediatric clocks. Each clock is comprised of a set of CpGs along with a weight assigned to each of these CpGs. The estimated age is a function of these weights and the methylation level at each of these CpGs. As such, in order to apply each of these clocks, we supplied the clock function with the methylation levels of the relevant CpGs for each individual infant. It is important to note that for all estimates, a minimum of 80% of all CpGs included in a clock were required to be present in an individual sample for an age estimate to be generated in accordance with thresholds set in existing literature as recommended to preserve the stability of age estimations (Pelegi-Siso et al., 2021). In the case of CpG missingness below this threshold, data for that CpG was imputed using Bioconductor’s KNN imputation method of imputing CpG methylation by using methylation data on the nearest neighbors of that CpG (Hastie et al., 1999; Troyanskaya et al., 2001).

### Statistical Analyses

All analyses were conducted in R version 4.2.1. In summary, epigenetic age as estimated separately in each clock was evaluated as a function of maternal urinary arsenic level in each cohort. In all analyses, we defined clinical chronological age as the estimated number of weeks of gestation for a newborn. As described above, epigenetic age (ie epigenetic gestational age and epigenetic pediatric age) was calculated as a function of methylation of CpGs determined to be predictive of age and all age estimations were calculated using the methylclock Bioinformatics package (Pelegi-Siso et al., 2021).

To evaluate the role of gestational arsenic exposure on gestational age, we evaluated epigenetic gestational age estimations as a function of maternal urinary arsenic in the US-based population. Total maternal inorganic urinary arsenic concentration in mothers was used as the proxy exposure for in utero arsenic. We separate groups into high and low arsenic exposure; differences in gestational and pediatric age were assessed using a student t-test. Adjusted p-values refer to Bonferroni corrected p-values. Mean gestational age in individuals in the lowest quartile of arsenic was computed and compared to average gestational age in individuals in the highest quartile of in utero arsenic exposure in the US population. After calculation of mean estimated age within each arsenic exposure group separately in all seven clocks, we conducted student t-tests for each clock to determine whether there were statistically significant differences in epigenetic age within arsenic exposure category. We also replicated these analyses in the smaller Mexico-based population to evaluate whether noted trends persisted outside of this US-based population. Estimated epigenetic age in each clock was treated as the outcome and arsenic exposure category (high vs low) was our primary predictor. In these models we adjusted for measured covariates that might confound the relationship between urinary arsenic and epigenetic age. The covariates we controlled for were maternal age, maternal smoking, maternal diabetes, infant clinical gestational age, and levels of other metals detected in placental samples (aluminum, chromium, cobalt, nickel, lead and selenium).

In addition, we conducted sensitivity analyses to evaluate the potential effect of unmeasured confounding on our results. To do this, we have used an E-Value based approach to estimating the necessary magnitude of effect that an unmeasured confounder would need to have with both the exposure and the outcome, to explain the observed relationship between exposure and outcome. The E-Value calculation was implemented using the EValue R package methods described by Van Der Weele and Ding (Mathur et al., 2018; Van Der Weele & Ding, 2017). Using the observed regression coefficient, the standard error of the coefficient, and the standard deviation of the outcome, we estimated the range of associations between an unmeasured confounder and both gestational age and arsenic exposure necessary to explain the observed relationship between exposure and outcome

## Results

### Characteristics of Study Populations

Arsenic exposure was higher in the Mexico-based population than the US-based population. Median arsenic levels measured in maternal urine collected during pregnancy were 30.19 μg/L (sd 78.90) in the Mexican cohort and 3.72 μg/L (sd 10.77) in the US cohort (Figure 1).

### Correlations across epigenetic gestational clock age and clinical gestational age

For both populations, we estimated gestational age using a panel of five gestational age clocks. After generating these estimates, we evaluated the correlations between gestational age estimates and clinical gestational ages. We observed that certain gestational clocks yielded estimates of epigenetic gestational age that displayed highly significant positive correlations with clinical gestational age (P < 0.05 in all correlations (Supplementary Figure 1). However, which clocks were most predictive of clinical gestational age varied as a function of population/tissue type. Specifically, the three Lee clocks of gestational age trained in placental tissue yielded high estimates of gestational age when applied to the placental tissue of the US population with R-squared values of 0.90, 0.85 and 0.94 for the Lee CPC, Lee RPC and Lee refined RPC clocks respectively (Figure 2).

The Lee clocks also correlated positively with clinical gestational age in the cord blood data of the Mexico population though the magnitude of these correlations is substantially reduced with R-squared values of 0.21, 0.10 and 0.11 for the Lee CPC, Lee RPC and Lee refined RPC clocks respectively. In addition, the Bohlin and Knight clocks of gestational age trained in cord blood were more predictive of clinical gestational age with Knight gestational age estimates having a R-squared value of 0.88 and the Bohlin clock having an R-squared value of 0.44. However, these two cord-blood trained clocks were not well correlated to gestational age when applied to placental tissue of the US population (Figure 2).

### Correlations across epigenetic pediatric clock age and clinical gestational age

For both populations, we also examined two pediatric clocks that were built with chronological age data from children and young adults aged 0 to 20 years old. We reasoned it would be informative to explore the behavior of these pediatric clocks in comparison to gestational age clocks, even though the samples studied here were taken at birth at which point all individuals have a chronological age of zero.

First, we observed that both pediatric clocks failed to yield correlations with clinical gestational age in either placental tissue of the US population or in cord blood tissue of the Mexican population. Furthermore, for the Wu clock trained in blood samples from individuals from chronological age 0 to 18, we find no correlation between its estimates of individual age and any of the other measures of epigenetic aging in the placental tissues of the US population. Interestingly though, for cord blood of the Mexican population, we found that Wu’s estimates of epigenetic aging are inversely associated with estimates of Lee’s estimates of gestational age. For the PedBE clock trained in buccal tissue from individuals aged 0 to 20, we observed no correlations with the three Lee clocks whereas we uncover positive correlations between the PedBE clock and Bohlin and Knight clocks of gestational age when applied to placental tissue (Figure 2).

### Epigenetic age as a function of maternal arsenic exposure in the US population

Clinical gestational age did not vary significantly between the high and low arsenic exposure groups within the US population (Table 3). In the US population, clinical gestational age was 39.34 weeks for infants with low arsenic exposure and 39.35 weeks for infants with high exposure (P = 0.971, Student t-test).

Despite this lack of variation in clinical gestational age, gestational age estimates generated using the Knight and Bohlin methods did display statistically significant variation when comparing infants with high arsenic exposure to those with low arsenic exposure, even after adjustment for multiple comparisons (P≤0.01) (Table 3). The average gestational age of high arsenic infants was 0.74 weeks lower in high arsenic infants when compared to low arsenic infants when evaluating Knight age estimates and 0.23 weeks lower when evaluating Bohlin age estimates (Figure 3). The magnitude of this difference was slightly increased after we adjusted for covariates and regressed estimated age on arsenic exposure level. After doing so, the average gestational age of high arsenic infants was 0.81 weeks lower in high arsenic infants when compared to low arsenic infants when comparing Knight age estimates and 0.24 weeks lower when comparing Bohlin age estimates (Table 4).

In contrast to our findings in gestational clocks, neither the Wu nor the PedBE pediatric clocks were able to detect a significant difference (P≤0.025) in epigenetic pediatric age when comparing high and low arsenic infants (Table 5a, Figure 4).

### Replication of epigenetic age analyses in association with maternal arsenic exposure in the Mexico-based population

In the population of infants from Mexico, clinical gestational age was 39.36 weeks for infants with low arsenic exposure and 38.40 weeks for infants with high arsenic exposure (P = 0.160, Student t-test). None of the estimated gestational ages were significantly different (P≤0.01) when comparing highly exposed infants to infants with lower exposures (Table 6). This is not surprising given the small sample size in this population. Noteworthy, however, the general trend across clock estimates in this population as well as the US population was congruent, showing that infants exposed to higher arsenic displayed average gestational ages that were lower than those of infants exposed to lower arsenic. The Lee CPC-based comparison in the US population was an exception to this trend with higher estimated gestational duration in high arsenic infants (this trend did not reach statistical significance). Similarly, the Lee ref RPC-based comparison was an exception to this trend with estimated gestational duration being the same in both arsenic exposure groups.

Interestingly, the Wu childhood clock-based estimation of epigenetic pediatric age was marginally significantly associated (P = 0.026) with arsenic exposure category when using an adjusted P-value cutoff to account for multiple testing (Table 5b). Specifically, infants exposed to higher arsenic displayed higher pediatric epigenetic age than infants exposed to lower arsenic during pregnancy despite the overall evidence that arsenic exposure is associated with lower gestational age.

## Discussion

Our findings indicate that arsenic exposure during gestation can impact the epigenome and epigenetic age as estimated with DNA methylation-based clocks. Specifically, our findings indicate that increased in utero arsenic exposure is associated with decreased gestational age. The trend of increased arsenic exposure being associated with decreased gestational age persisted in our replication analyses in the Mexico population, despite the small sample size of this population. In addition, in the population of infants from Mexico, the Wu clock estimates of pediatric age suggested that infants with higher arsenic exposure were significantly older at birth than their counterparts with lower exposure.

Previous work has indicated that epigenetic gestational age deceleration (ie, lower gestational age) is associated with adverse fetal exposures, including maternal gestational diabetes, maternal preeclampsia and increased PM2.5 exposure level (Ladd-Acosta, Vang, Barrett, Bulka, Bush, et al., 2023; Song et al., 2022). While these studies indicate the ability of gestational clocks to detect in utero exposure to stressors during gestation, to our knowledge this paper represents the first replication of this effect and observation of this response in relation to maternal arsenic exposure.

In addition, it is important to note that in contrast to interpretations of post-natal epigenetic age estimations in pediatric clocks, deceleration as estimated in gestational clocks is not an indication of lowered risk for adverse outcomes. To the contrary, gestational age deceleration in newborn tissues have been associated with lower birthweight and other adverse outcomes such as decreased lung function as measured by Apgar score and increased odds of developmental delay (Bright et al., 2019; Girchenko et al., 2017; Khouja et al., 2018; Polinski et al., 2023). In addition, while effects of decreased gestational length are more pronounced when comparing term infants (gestational age > 37 weeks) to preterm infants, shorter gestational lengths have been associated with attenuated neurodevelopment and lung function in childhood even among full-term pregnancies (Davis et al., 2011; Hansen et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2010).

An important caveat of this research is that epigenetic age estimates (ie, gestational age as well as pediatric and adult epigenetic ages) can vary from tissue to tissue within the same individual (Dieckmann et al., 2021). As such, epigenetic age estimates based on one tissue type may not always be indicative of the overall health or epigenetic age of a newborn. While we have not studied epigenetic age across several tissues from the same individual in this paper, we have evaluated trends in gestational and pediatric age within placenta and cord blood, two tissues of vital importance to fetal development. Interestingly, tissue type mismatch between the tissues wherein clocks were developed and the tissue to which these clocks were applied did seem to limit our ability to detect arsenic-associated patterns in gestational age. In fact, cord blood-based gestational clocks were most sensitive to arsenic in placenta tissue samples from US infants.

Taken altogether, our results indicate that arsenic exposure is likely to impact epigenetic gestational age among newborns and potentially influence post-natal pediatric epigenetic age too. Given the body of evidence in support of the ability of epigenetic clocks to detect disease risk for outcomes including various cancers, further longitudinal study of the relationship between in utero arsenic exposure and risk of adverse health outcomes may play a vital role in understanding risk profiles especially in communities at increased risk of arsenic exposure. However, further research with larger sample sizes is necessary to determine whether gestational epigenetic age estimations in newborns with arsenic exposure are consistent across tissues and whether gestational epigenetic age deceleration in response to arsenic exposure can be utilized to better understand risk in newborns exposed during gestation. It is also of note that there is always the possibility of unmeasured confounding in observational research in humans. Here we used an E-value based sensitivity analyses to assess this issue (Mathur et al., 2018; Van Der Weele & Ding, 2017). For the Bohlin clock the estimated E-value of the magnitude of unmeasured confounding was 2.37 while for the Knight value it was 2.49 (Supplementary Figure 1). Given that the confounder (clinical gestational age) with the largest statistically significant magnitude in this analysis of the relationship between arsenic and epigenetic gestational age had a point estimate of 0.93, we conclude that our findings are unlikely to be explained by an unmeasured confounder.

In addition, further analysis is needed to determine whether the trends observed in this US population persist in other populations with even more varied arsenic exposure. While the replication analysis in the Mexico-based population is promising and displays congruence with the findings in the US population, further replication is required in other populations with larger sample sizes. Further, given the potential for SNP alleles tied to ancestry to erroneously be interpreted as differences in DNA methylation, the multifactorial effects of race and class as well as environmental heterogeneity across regions, it is important for this question to be evaluated in populations of varied ancestries, nationalities and races. Given the lack of racial and national diversity in this population, it is unclear whether the findings of this study can be generalized to other populations.

Despite these limitations and opportunities for future study, this study represents an important step in characterizing the effects of in utero arsenic exposure on gestational age. Given the high global burden of arsenic exposure and the sensitivity of the gestational period, understanding the impact of in utero arsenic exposure on gestational age and downstream outcomes is an important step to assessing and understanding risk to newborns and the pregnant population and setting appropriate guidelines and action levels for arsenic levels in the environment.

Finally, it is worthwhile to consider the impact of arsenic exposure during pregnancy on long term post-natal epigenetic aging. An interestingly possibility is that in utero exposure during pregnancy not only results in reduced gestational age and reduced fetal maturity but also sets exposed newborns on a trajectory of accelerated aging upon birth. The notion is supported by the data presented here as well as by well-described evidence of lower birth weight and lung under-development and dysfunction in arsenic exposed newborns (Kile et al., 2016; Quansah et al., 2015; Ramsey et al., 2013; Salmeri et al., 2020). This notion is also supported by an excess of hypermethylated sites at CpG islands and genic regions in arsenic exposed newborns (Lumour-Mensah & Lemos, 2023), a feature that is further indication of accelerated pediatric age. Collectively, the data raise the prospects that arsenic exposed populations might display accelerated post-natal epigenetic aging, potentially starting at birth.
